chapters.title: Design a product worth making
chapters.goal: Land on one original product you can describe clearly, that solves a real want or need better than what already exists.
explanation: Start from something you'd genuinely want to own yourself — a specific design, a better version of something ordinary, a product for a hobby you're part of.
Research 5-10 similar products already for sale — note their price, quality complaints in reviews, and what a better version would actually change.
Sketch or prototype the simplest possible first version — resist designing 10 variants before you've made and held even one.
Order or make a single sample before committing to anything else — most real problems (fit, material feel, function) only show up once it's physical.
Write your one-sentence pitch: "Unlike [existing option], mine [specific difference] because [reason]."
chapters.example: Yael was frustrated that reusable water bottles with fun designs always cracked at the lid. She researched competitors' 1-star reviews (lid cracking was the #1 complaint), designed a reinforced lid, and ordered one sample before deciding on colors or branding.
mistakes: Designing multiple product variants before making and testing even one sample.
Skipping competitor research and missing an easy, specific differentiator hiding in their bad reviews.
Falling in love with a design before checking if it's actually better than what already exists, not just different.
chapters.template:
Product worksheet:
Product idea: ____
Competitor research — common complaint in reviews: "____"
My specific improvement: "____"
One-sentence pitch: "Unlike [X], mine [Y] because [Z]."
checklist: Researched 5-10 similar existing products and their reviews
Identified a specific, real improvement over existing options
Made or ordered one physical sample before deciding anything else
Wrote the one-sentence pitch

chapters.title: Know exactly who buys this
chapters.goal: Describe the specific person who'd choose your product over a cheaper or more established alternative.
explanation: Your buyer isn't "anyone who needs [category]" — it's someone with a specific reason to prefer YOUR version, often tied directly to the improvement you identified.
Read reviews (positive and negative) of competitor products to understand exactly what this buyer already cares about and complains about.
Find where this buyer already spends time (a hobby community, a specific social platform, a local group) rather than guessing.
Write a short profile: who they are, what they currently use instead, and the one sentence that would make them switch.
Show your sample/prototype to 3-5 real people matching this profile and note their actual reaction, not just polite feedback.
chapters.example: Yael's buyer profile: "People who've already owned a cheap reusable bottle that cracked, who care about durability more than trend, and hang out in zero-waste/sustainability communities online." Her messaging led with durability, not aesthetics.
mistakes: Targeting "everyone who drinks water" instead of the specific person with a reason to prefer this version.
Guessing what the audience cares about instead of reading their real reviews of similar products.
Only asking friends for feedback instead of people who actually match the target buyer profile.
chapters.template:
Audience one-pager:
Who: ____
What they currently use instead: ____
What makes them switch: "____"
Where they hang out: ____
checklist: Read reviews of competitor products for real audience pain points
Wrote the specific buyer profile
Found where this buyer already spends time online
Showed the sample to 3-5 people matching the profile

chapters.title: Price for real margin
chapters.goal: Set a price that covers your true per-unit cost with enough margin to survive returns, fees and slow periods.
explanation: Calculate the true per-unit cost: manufacturing/materials, packaging, and shipping to you — not just the raw material price.
A common approach for an original product is pricing at 2.5-4× true cost, since you're carrying more risk (unsold inventory) than a dropshipper.
Compare to 3-5 competitor prices and place yourself within a sensible range — a much lower price on an "improved" product looks suspicious rather than like a deal.
Account for payment processor fees (roughly 3%) and expected return/defect rate when calculating real margin, not just the sale price minus cost.
Decide your break-even unit count — how many units you need to sell to recover your batch cost — before ordering stock.
chapters.example: Yael's bottle cost $6.50 landed per unit for a 50-unit batch. At 3.5× that's about $22.75; she priced at $24, checked against $18-32 competitor range, and calculated she needed to sell 14 units just to recover the batch cost.
mistakes: Pricing based on what feels fair rather than the real cost-plus-margin math.
Forgetting to account for returns/defects when calculating real margin.
Not knowing the break-even unit count before ordering a batch.
chapters.template:
Pricing calculator:
True landed cost per unit: $____
Cost × 3 = suggested price: $____
Competitor range: $____ – $____
My price: $____
Break-even units needed to recover batch cost: ____
checklist: Calculated true landed cost per unit
Applied the multiplier and compared to competitors
Accounted for processor fees and expected returns
Calculated break-even unit count before ordering

chapters.title: Batch size and startup costs
chapters.goal: Order the smallest batch that lets you actually sell and learn, without risking money you can't afford to lose.
explanation: Unlike dropshipping, you pay for stock upfront — this is real money at risk before any sale happens, so budget and batch size decisions matter more here than almost anywhere else in this app.
Always order the smallest batch a supplier allows for your first run, even if the per-unit price is worse — proving demand matters more than maximizing margin on an unproven product.
Budget for the full real cost: manufacturing, shipping to you, packaging, and a small buffer for defects — not just the quoted unit price.
Set a hard total spending cap you (and a parent, if their money/card is involved) are fully prepared to lose if the product doesn't sell.
Get a second sample from your chosen manufacturer before the full batch ships, to catch quality issues before they're baked into 50+ units.
chapters.example: Yael's supplier's minimum batch was 50 units at $6.50 landed each — $325 total. Her parents agreed to a $400 hard cap (batch plus a small buffer), fully understanding it could all be lost if the bottles didn't sell.
mistakes: Ordering a large batch for a better per-unit price before any real demand is proven.
Forgetting to budget for packaging and shipping-to-you costs on top of the manufacturing price.
Skipping a pre-batch quality-check sample and discovering a defect only after 50+ units arrive.
chapters.template:
Startup budget sheet:
Smallest batch size supplier allows: ____ units
Total batch cost (incl. shipping/packaging): $____
Hard cap I'm prepared to lose entirely: $____
Pre-batch quality sample ordered? Yes/No
checklist: Ordered the smallest batch size the supplier allows
Budgeted the full real cost, not just quoted unit price
Set a hard spending cap agreed with a parent if their money is involved
Got a quality-check sample before the full batch
chapters.parentNote: A physical product batch is real upfront money at risk, and most suppliers/payment methods for bulk ordering need an adult. A parent should agree the spending cap in writing before any batch is ordered.

chapters.title: Build a brand around the product
chapters.goal: Give the product a name, story and look that make it feel like a real, considered brand, not a random item.
explanation: Pick a name that's easy to say and remember, and check it's not already a registered trademark or an existing well-known brand in your category.
Design consistent packaging or presentation — even a simple branded sticker or card insert makes a product feel intentional rather than generic.
Write the story behind why you made this — the real problem that led to it (from chapter 1) — since a genuine story differentiates far more than generic marketing copy.
Take real, honest product photos showing actual use, not just studio shots — for a physical product, buyers want to see it in the real world.
Decide your return/quality policy up front and state it clearly — it's one of the biggest trust signals for a small, unknown brand.
chapters.example: Yael named her bottles "Holdfast", included a small card in every package explaining the lid-cracking problem she set out to fix, and photographed real people using the bottles at school and the gym instead of only studio shots.
mistakes: Generic, unbranded packaging that makes the product feel like an unbranded dropship item.
Skipping the real story behind the product in favor of generic marketing language.
No clear return/quality policy stated anywhere, which reads as untrustworthy for a new brand.
chapters.template:
Brand one-pager:
Name (checked for conflicts): ____
Packaging/presentation: ____
One-paragraph real story: "____"
Return/quality policy in one sentence: "____"
checklist: Picked a name and checked for conflicts
Designed simple, consistent packaging or presentation
Wrote the real story behind the product
Stated a clear return/quality policy

chapters.title: Choose where to sell
chapters.goal: Pick the right mix of storefront and marketing channel for a physical, original product.
explanation: A marketplace with built-in buyers (like Etsy for handmade/design goods) can get you sales faster than a standalone store with zero traffic — consider starting there, or alongside your own store.
Match your marketing channel to your audience profile — visual/lifestyle products usually do well with real-use photo and video content on social platforms.
Whichever primary channel you pick, install analytics/tracking before spending any money on ads, so you can see what's actually working.
Consider selling a small amount locally first (friends, school, a local market/fair) — it's a fast, low-risk way to get real feedback and your first reviews.
Don't spread your limited first batch across too many channels at once — concentrate early sales and reviews in one or two places.
chapters.example: Yael listed on Etsy (built-in buyers already searching for sustainable products) and posted real-use content on Instagram, driving traffic to the same Etsy listing rather than splitting effort across a separate store too.
mistakes: Building a standalone store with no existing traffic instead of considering a marketplace with built-in buyers first.
Spreading a small first batch across too many channels, diluting reviews and momentum everywhere.
Spending on ads before installing basic tracking to see what's working.
chapters.template:
Channel plan:
Primary channel: ____ (marketplace / own store / local)
Secondary marketing channel: ____
Tracking installed before spending? Yes/No
checklist: Picked a primary sales channel matching the audience
Considered a marketplace with built-in buyers for the first batch
Installed tracking before any ad spend
Concentrated the first batch's sales in one or two channels, not many

chapters.title: Sell your first units
chapters.goal: Get real strangers to buy, and collect the reviews and feedback that make the next sale easier.
explanation: Make sure checkout and shipping logistics actually work by placing a test order yourself, or having a friend do so, before driving real traffic.
For a new, unproven brand, consider a small honest launch incentive (a modest discount for early reviewers) to get your first real reviews faster.
Ship carefully and promptly — for a physical product, the unboxing experience itself is part of what gets shared and reviewed.
Follow up directly with early buyers to ask for a review once they've had time to actually use the product, not immediately after shipping.
Log everything about each early sale: what channel it came from, what almost stopped them (if they mention it), and what they said afterward.
chapters.example: Yael's first five sales came through a launch discount shared with a sustainability Instagram community she'd been genuinely part of for months — not strangers, but people who already trusted her presence there.
mistakes: Driving traffic to checkout before testing that the actual purchase and shipping flow works end to end.
Asking for a review immediately at shipping instead of after the buyer has actually used the product.
Not tracking where early sales actually came from, losing the ability to double down on what worked.
chapters.template:
First-sales log:
Test order placed myself? Yes/No
Sale source | What almost stopped them | Review received?
checklist: Tested checkout and shipping myself before launch
Considered a launch incentive for early reviewers
Shipped carefully and promptly with attention to unboxing
Logged the source and outcome of each early sale

chapters.title: Handle stock, shipping and issues
chapters.goal: Manage inventory and problems responsibly so a growing brand doesn't outrun its own reliability.
explanation: Track exact stock levels and never sell what you don't have — an oversold, backordered item creates a review that stays forever.
Set honest shipping-time expectations on the listing and stick to them — a delay you warned about is fine; a silent one isn't.
Have a clear, pre-decided process for damaged/wrong items — replace or refund quickly rather than making a customer argue their case.
Watch remaining stock against your reorder lead time — running out completely while waiting weeks for a restock loses momentum and sales.
Keep a simple spreadsheet of stock in, stock sold, and stock remaining, updated after every sale.
chapters.example: When Yael's stock dropped to 10 units, she ordered a restock immediately rather than waiting until zero, since her supplier's lead time was three weeks — she never had to pause sales.
mistakes: Selling units you don't actually have in stock, creating backorder frustration.
Waiting until stock hits zero to reorder, causing an avoidable sales gap.
Making a customer prove fault before resolving a damaged or wrong item.
chapters.template:
Stock and service playbook:
Current stock: ____  Reorder lead time: ____ weeks  Reorder trigger point: ____ units
Damaged/wrong item policy: "____"
checklist: Set up a simple stock tracking sheet
Set an honest shipping-time expectation on the listing
Wrote a clear damaged/wrong item policy
Set a reorder trigger point based on lead time

chapters.title: Payments and checkout
chapters.goal: Accept payment safely and legally for a physical product business.
explanation: Payment processors and most marketplaces require an 18+ account holder — under that age, a parent opens and holds the account, with you running the store day to day.
Agree the payout schedule and destination account with the account-holding parent before sales start.
Keep basic fraud protection (address verification, card verification) turned on — it's usually on by default.
Keep a simple record of every sale, refund and fee, which you'll need for the accounting chapter.
Never share payment account details or one-time codes with anyone claiming to be a supplier or platform "support" over chat.
chapters.example: Yael's Etsy shop and Stripe account for her own site were both opened under her mother's name, with a written agreement that profit transferred to Yael's account monthly after costs.
mistakes: Trying to work around the 18+ requirement, which risks funds being frozen for a terms-of-service breach.
Not agreeing on the payout schedule before sales start.
Sharing account details or codes with anyone in a message claiming to need them for "verification."
chapters.template:
Payment setup record:
Processor/marketplace account holder (18+): ____
Agreed payout schedule: ____
Where I log every sale/refund/fee: ____
checklist: Payment/marketplace account opened by an adult 18+
Agreed payout schedule in writing with that adult
Confirmed basic fraud protection is on
Set up a simple sales/refund/fee log
chapters.parentNote: Payment processors and most marketplaces require an 18+ account holder almost everywhere. This chapter needs a parent to open and hold that account.

chapters.title: Accounting and taxes
chapters.goal: Track real profit (not just revenue) and know what's owed, including inventory costs.
explanation: Business income is taxable in almost every country, including for minors, and physical-product businesses also need to track inventory cost, not just sales — rules vary by country.
Keep a running log: date, sale amount, unit cost, shipping cost, processor fee, and any refunds — profit is revenue minus ALL of these, not just revenue minus unit cost.
Remember unsold inventory sitting in a box is money already spent, not profit — don't count it as available cash until it's actually sold.
Set aside a percentage of real profit (a rough 25-30% placeholder is common) rather than spending all sales revenue as it comes in.

Have one real conversation with a parent, and once income is more than pocket change, check your country's actual rules for minors' business income, plus whether product safety/labelling rules apply to your specific product category.
chapters.example: Yael's spreadsheet tracked revenue, unit cost, shipping, and fees separately every month, and she set aside 30% of real profit — while remembering the 15 unsold bottles still in her closet weren't cash yet.
mistakes: Counting unsold inventory as available profit instead of money already spent.
Tracking only revenue, not true profit after all real costs.
Not checking whether product safety or labelling rules apply to the specific product category.
chapters.template:
Bookkeeping log (one row per sale):
Date | Sale amount | Unit cost | Shipping | Processor fee | Refund | Net
Monthly: revenue $____ − costs $____ = profit $____ → set aside ____% = $____
checklist: Started a running sales/cost log including inventory cost
Distinguished true profit from revenue and unsold stock
Set aside a percentage of real profit
Checked whether product safety/labelling rules apply to my product
chapters.parentNote: Physical-product business income and inventory tracking involve real legal and tax questions that depend on your country and product category. This needs a parent involved and, once income is real, a proper check with a tax authority or accountant.

chapters.title: Growing the brand
chapters.goal: Turn one proven product into a small, repeatable, slowly-scaling brand.
explanation: Once you've sold through a first batch, look at real patterns: which channel, which content, which specific claim (durability, design, story) actually drove sales.
Reinvest a planned portion of profit into a slightly larger next batch of the proven product before adding new products — prove repeatability first.
Once you have real reviews and social proof, you can often raise price slightly without losing conversion — reviews do real selling work.
Consider a second product only once the first is a genuinely reliable, repeatable seller, not because you're bored of the first one.
Review weekly: sell-through rate, return rate, and real profit per batch — not just total revenue, which can hide a shrinking margin.
chapters.example: After selling through her first 50 units in six weeks with a 4% return rate, Yael ordered a 150-unit second batch of the same bottle — proven repeatable — before even sketching a second product.
mistakes: Launching a second product before the first is a proven, repeatable seller.
Reinvesting profit without a plan, instead of pointing it at what's already proven to work.
Watching only total revenue and missing a shrinking real margin underneath it.
chapters.template:
Weekly growth review:
Sell-through rate: ____%  Return rate: ____%  Real profit per batch: $____
Best-performing channel/claim: ____
This week's one decision: reorder / new product / hold steady
checklist: Identified the real pattern behind what's driving sales
Reinvested profit into a proven repeat batch before a new product
Considered a modest price increase once real reviews existed
Set up a weekly review of sell-through, returns and real profit
